rv.q: Anon isn’t a particularly warmhearted play — nor need it be — but as Delia works on writing her own soliloquy for a Shakespearean character who doesn’t have one (she chooses Lear’s daughter Goneril), Washburn’s empathy reveals itself as a matter of artistry.
I found the second act less rewarding, and inconclusive, as the play becomes more fantastical and stylized.
For once in a Washburn play, the meta-theatrical link refuses to make contact; the mixture doesn’t gel.
But there’s a twist in this quirky, engaging piece, now in its world premiere off-Broadway at MCC Theater.
In its premiere at MCC Theater, ANON transcends this familiar domestic setting as the virtual world of screens, sounds, images, and conspiracies threatens to overwhelm the physical one.
Her performance and that of the rest of the intense cast, along with Washburn’s insightful portrait of our media-mad society make for a thought-provoking, but not entirely satisfactory experience.
Washburn has an uncanny ability to tiptoe up to rich dramatic situations without ever seeing them through.
But for all its dramatic ambitions, nothing is resolved and the production leaves the characters and the audience hanging, strangely unmoved.
It’s a shame, then, that Anon seems content to coast on the surface of its provocative situations.

Once or twice, ANON looks like it might generate some sizzle, especially when Delia confronts Jeanie for posting an easily discredited allegation regarding the Holocaust, but most of the time it is too scattered to have any impact.
It is an important reminder of shared humanity and the importance of valuing one another before someone decides to seek that validation somewhere else in desperation.
The play crackles with life in the first act.

The play is admirably ambitious, overlaying the story of the indoctrinated Jeanie and her family and neighbors with motifs and scenes from Shakespeare’s King Lear, though the results are mixed: ideas and characters feel as though they are still in the process of being worked out.
The play has confusing elements in the script which are never clarified.
But while actual QAnon believers wait for the storm, theatergoers get only a rumble of thunder.
In the end, Anon lacks the specificity to bring its central character fully to life and out of the shadows of anonymity.

cn.t: Washburn's QAnon drama draws praise for Crystal Finn's performance and timely subject matter, but critics find the play scattershot and unfocused, with a strong first act that fizzles into an unsatisfying second act resolution.

vr.q: It's a shame that it falls apart in Act 2.
